ingredients.intro: The listing prints a Latin ingredient line of five plants. It does not say whether those five are all of them, and it does not name the part used for any of them. Here is what each plant is, where it grows, and which part of it the trade usually sells. We hold no photograph of any of the five, so those frames are empty rather than filled with a stand-in, and any picture on this page that is a generated scene says so.

cards.p: A woody climbing vine of Costa Rica, Colombia and Ecuador that scrambles through forest on prickly stems. The long root and rhizome are the part traded. Sarsaparilla is a trade name that covers several Smilax species rather than one, and this listing names one of them, which is more than most sarsaparilla on sale manages.

A tall biennial of Eurasian roadsides and waste ground, in the daisy family, with big rhubarb-like leaves in the first year and hooked burrs in the second. Those burrs, caught in a dog's coat, are what gave a Swiss engineer the idea for hook and loop fastening. The root is the part usually sold, in Japan as gobo, and it is the burdock of dandelion and burdock. The listing spells the genus Articum; the accepted spelling is Arctium.

A deep-rooted perennial weed of European field edges, now naturalised almost everywhere, named for the crimped wavy margin of its leaves. It carries rust-brown seed spikes that stand through the winter. The root is the part usually sold. It is a plant high in oxalate, which is the reason for the note on the sheet below.

The broad-trunked African tree with branches that look like roots in the air. Its fruit hangs in a hard velvety pod and the pulp inside dries on the tree by itself, so it is milled to a pale powder without any drying step at all. Which is unusual enough to be worth saying about a plant.

A low sprawling annual of gardens, allotments and waste ground across the temperate world, with a single line of hairs running up one side of the stem and tiny white flowers whose five deeply split petals look like ten. The whole plant above ground is the part usually gathered.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: Five plants are named here in Latin, one of them corrected against the listing's spelling, and the milligrams, the count, the serving and the day rate are all printed. Where the listing carries a figure nobody has measured, the row says so instead. Mag Flux is the name on the jar. It is a name, not a description, and we do not expand it.

reiss.label: Reiss's turn
reiss.h2: Why the mineral lines came off this page
paras: The old listing for this jar states that it contains iron, zinc and B vitamins, and then says what each of those is meant to do. Both halves came off. Not because the plants are wrong, but because nobody has measured this jar. Without a number from a test, a mineral sentence is decoration, and decoration is exactly what I do not want on a specification sheet.

The one place on this whole site where a mineral figure survives is Seaking, because there is an actual measurement per capsule behind it. That is the standard: a number, from a test, tied to the formula it is printed on. When this jar has one, it goes on the sheet the same day.

There is a second thing worth correcting in the open. The listing's prose talks about dandelion and burdock. Burdock, Arctium lappa, is on the ingredient line. Dandelion is not on it at all. Somebody wrote a good sentence and nobody checked it against the list underneath.

The Latin is misspelled on the listing as well, Articum for Arctium. It is a small thing. It is also the kind of small thing that tells you whether anyone checked, so it is corrected on the sheet above with the change marked rather than done quietly.
reiss.pull: A good sentence is not an ingredient.
